extracted.intended_audience: classical scholars, students, and editors preparing editions/translations of Horace
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing a critical edition and English translation of Horace's Satires, Epistles, and Ars Poetica, including dating, literary interpretation, manuscript collation, and use of commentaries and secondary scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make translation into more than a mere translation / approach as new edition
rubrics_metrics.description: The book should be something more than a mere translation — something approaching a new edition of the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an Introduction for each Satire and Epistle; indicate sequence of thought when Horace's transitions are abrupt; explain numerous allusions in notes or Index; discuss dubious passages (however briefly); scrutinize the Latin text in every detail; register all important variant readings; utilize results of both old and recent scholarship in translation or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dating poems by internal historical and literary allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish probable dates/publication order by reference within the poems to other works, patrons, and political events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit allusions (e.g., to Virgil's Eclogues, to Maecenas), mentions of historical events or offices (e.g., Dacians, Battle of Actium, temple of Janus, triumphs, consulships like Lollius, Agrippa's campaigns, Tiberius' progress) and absence of expected allusions to bound publication windows. Cross-check with known dates of related works (Epodes, Odes) and scholarly proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify satiric genre origins and distinguishing formal features
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a satire derives from dramatic/rustic farce or the later literary (read-for-reading) tradition and note its metrical and topical miscellany.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for signs of dramatic origin (performative exodae, afterplays) versus literary miscellany; assess the presence of mixed metres and variety of subjects, autobiographical elements, philosophical discourse, mock-heroic or Priapic material, and whether the work was intended for acting or private reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess Lucilius' influence on Horace
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the degree to which Horace imitates, adapts, or departs from Lucilius across vocabulary, tone, themes, and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare thematic parallels (autobiography, invective, philosophical topics), diction (use of Gallic/Etruscan/Syrian and Italic dialect words in Lucilius), metrical choices, satiric moulding, instances where Horace adopts or rejects Lucilian coarseness or invective. Use fragmentary evidence of Lucilius to reconstruct models when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret satiric tone and authorial intent (defence vs. attack)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a satire functions as a defence of the genre/author or as an offensive invective, and how it negotiates Roman libel/legal constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider poems addressing criticism of satire (defences in Satires I.3, I.4, II.1 etc.), explicit statements about freedom of speech, references to libel laws, and whether the poet adopts genial urbanity versus coarse, personal attack. Relate tone to the poet's stage of career (earlier Lucilian mimicry vs later Horatian urbanity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date Ars Poetica and infer compositional history from internal and manuscript evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use manuscript placement, stylistic affinities (notably to Lucilius), and intertextual echoes to estimate composition date and editorial history of Ars Poetica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that Mss place Ars Poetica variably (after Carmen Saeculare or Odes IV); consider hypothesis that it may have been written earlier and later adjusted to epistolary form; use parallels with Lucilius as evidence for earlier composition; weigh seventeenth–nineteenth-century editorial decisions (e.g., Cruquius labeling it Third Epistle) in establishing transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript classification and precedence rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Group extant manuscripts into families/classes derived from lost archetypes and prefer readings according to their distribution and perceived archetypal value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a stemmatic approach (e.g., Keller & Holder's three classes; Vollmer's two groups I & II; Garrod's simplifications). Give precedence to a reading found in mss of two classes over that found in only one; consider age (uncial vs cursive), completeness, and systematic alterations/interpolations when assessing value. Recognize limitations: most Horatian mss are cursive and none earlier than the 9th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ancient scholia and commentaries as textual witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ Porphyrio, Acron, and Cruquius' marginalia as earlier evidence to determine priority of conflicting readings and to explain textual problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat scholia as valuable because they precede many manuscripts, but be alert to interpolations and late strata (Acron surviving texts as late as 5th century). Use the Commentator Cruquianus material from the lost Blandinian mss to recover readings otherwise lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and principles of textual reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to reconstruct back toward an original archetype but acknowledge practical limits beyond certain editorial ancestors (e.g., Mavortian edition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Bentley/Vollmer principles in reconstructing a presumed early archetype; recognize that reconstruction beyond the sixth-century Mavortian layer is speculative. Use a balanced approach: prefer simpler, sound stemmata and avoid overcomplicated classifications that lack general acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for choosing and valuing modern editions and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Select modern editions based on thoroughness of collation, reliability of apparatus criticus, informed manuscript selection, and useful annotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical reputation (Bentley, Keller & Holder, Vollmer), the editor's manuscript choices (which mss were adopted or omitted), presence of a serviceable apparatus criticus, and the quality of explanatory notes. Note that editor judgments (e.g., Cruquius' vetustissimus) may be questioned; weigh editors' emendations against manuscript and scholia evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literary-historical evidence to classify individual satires
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify individual poems (e.g., which are Lucilian models, which show Horatian independence, which belong to particular subgenres like cena satirica or Priapeum) by internal content and external parallels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine subject-matter (e.g., courtroom scene, erotic/coarse content, dinner-scenes), vocabulary and intertextual echoes (Terence, Lucilius), autobiographical elements, and whether the poem functions as polemic, defence of art, parody, or genre-mixing. Use these features to position poems within Horace's development and within satiric subgenres.
